en: The Jātaka:
The Twelfth Chapter,
The Minor Section on Kuṇāla.
3. The Jātaka of the Sea-Going Merchant:
“Those people plough and sow, for human beings live by the fruit of their actions.”
“We do not share in this island;
for us, this very Jambudvīpa is our boon.
When the moon had been present for three or five nights—
"The force of the ocean will become great;
I shall overflow this vast island.
Do not let him slay you; go to another refuge!"
“Never indeed shall the surge of the ocean’s waters overflow this sublime island;
for that has been seen by me through many omens.”
Do not fear; why do you grieve?
Be glad! This excellent dwelling has been placed at your disposal, with abundant food and plentiful drink.
"I see no cause for fear in you at all;
rejoice, O you who have sons and grandsons!
"That deity who is here in the southern quarter..."
Khemā summons him with truth:
"The Higher One knows fear and fearlessness;
do not be afraid, why do you grieve? Rejoice!"
“Just as these spirits speak at variance—
one proclaiming fear and another safety—
listen now, I pray, to my words.”
"Let us all not perish quickly and lightly.
Let us all come together and build a ship—
a sturdy boat equipped with all necessary gear."
If this one on the right speaks the truth,
then this one on the left speaks falsely; thus,
that very [truth] will serve us as a means for resolving the crisis.
"And we shall not abandon this island.
But if Uttara has spoken the truth,
then this gift of the South is in vain."
Having boarded that very boat,
may we all thus cross safely to the further shore.
Indeed, it is not easy for one who grasps at the first [shore] to reach the best.
Having taken what has come within the range of one's younger [senses],
that person who here discriminates and grasps what is true indeed reaches the highest state.
Just as those merchants, in the midst of the ocean waters, were carried safely by their own karma, so too,
having penetrated the meaning of what was yet to come—
Even a little he does not transcend, though he possesses vast wisdom.
But fools, through delusion and greed for flavors,
do not penetrate the goal that lies in the future.
They falter when misfortunes arise in the present,
like those men in the midst of the ocean.
One should prepare for what must be done in the future.
“‘Do not let me fail in my duty at the time when duty must be done’—
for one such as that who performs his duty at the proper time,
no failure in duty occurs at the time when duty must be done.”
The Third Jātaka: The Story of the Sea-Going Merchant.
